title: Sharks Where They Shouldn't Be. #1 Lives Inside a Volcano
description: This week, Busan finally guided a 3-meter dusky shark out of a city canal after more than a month and 1.6 million visitors. But that's not even the strangest place sharks turn up. We count down five, from a golf course lake to sharks 4,200 km up the Amazon, a shark that walks on land, and hammerheads living inside an active volcano.

scenes.say: A shark just lived in a city canal for a month. And over a million people came to watch.

scenes.label: This week
scenes.say: Okay, so this happened in Busan, South Korea, and the city only got it out this week.

scenes.label: Not even close
scenes.say: But here's the thing. It's not the strangest place a shark has ever shown up. Not even close.

scenes.label: Five places
scenes.say: So today, five places sharks really should not be. And stay to the very end, because number one is the strangest.

scenes.label: Stay for #1
scenes.say: It's a place that should cook any animal alive. Burning hot, full of acid. Sharks live there anyway.

scenes.label: Counting down
scenes.say: We're counting down, and each one is weirder than the last. Ready? Let's go.

scenes.label: City canal
scenes.say: Number five. A shark in the middle of a city. Not a beach. A city.

scenes.label: Mid-September
scenes.say: In mid-September, people in Busan spotted a big gray fin in a man-made canal near the North Port.

scenes.label: About 3 meters
scenes.say: It was a dusky shark. A female, about three meters long. That's nearly ten feet, in water only about three meters deep.

scenes.label: Meet Bukangi
scenes.say: Fans gave her a name. Bukangi, after the Korean name for Busan's North Port.

scenes.label: 1.6 million visitors
scenes.say: And she became a celebrity. More than 1.6 million visitors came to the canal to see her.

scenes.label: A whole city
scenes.say: Think about that. A whole city stopping by a canal, just to watch one fin go back and forth.

scenes.label: Wrong home
scenes.say: Here's the problem, though. Dusky sharks are a warm-water species. A city canal is no home for her.

scenes.label: Not eating
scenes.say: Experts said she hadn't been seen eating. She even seemed to struggle to keep her balance. And the water was getting colder.

scenes.label: Attempt one
scenes.say: So the city tried to get her out. On September 29, boats sprayed jets of water. She just dodged them.

scenes.label: Attempt two
scenes.say: On October 2, they stretched nets across the canal. She swam right over the top.

scenes.label: Clock ticking
scenes.say: So now the clock was ticking. Every cold night made it worse for her.

scenes.label: October 21
scenes.say: Finally, on October 21, workers moved nets on floating platforms, slowly, for hours. And they guided her out toward the sea.

scenes.label: Free at last
scenes.say: The mayor wrote, we hope Bukangi can live a healthy life in the blue sea. She was later seen near a pier.

scenes.label: Warming seas
scenes.say: And one professor in Busan said sharks in South Korean waters are not common at all. Environmental groups blame warming seas.

scenes.label: Golf course
scenes.say: Number four. Sharks on a golf course. Yes, a golf course, with sand traps and little carts.

scenes.label: Real sharks
scenes.say: I'm serious. In Australia, there's a golf course with a lake next to the fairways. And for years, that lake had bull sharks in it.

scenes.label: 1991 to 1996
scenes.say: How did they get there? Floods. Between 1991 and 1996, floods pushed nearby rivers over their banks, and the sharks got carried inland.

scenes.label: Trapped
scenes.say: When the water dropped, they were stuck. In a pond. Surrounded by golfers, every single day.

scenes.label: Nearly 20 years
scenes.say: And they didn't just survive. They grew up to three meters long, and they stayed for nearly twenty years.

scenes.label: Lost ball?
scenes.say: Imagine losing your ball in that water. Would you go in to get it? I wouldn't.

scenes.label: Fins on the course
scenes.say: People actually saw fins cutting through the water while they played. Nobody ever made a formal count of how many sharks were in there.

scenes.label: Last seen 2015
scenes.say: They were last seen in 2015. Scientists think some escaped in a 2013 flood, and others probably died there.

scenes.label: A record
scenes.say: A recent study told their whole story. The team says it's the longest known case of bull sharks living nonstop in low-salt water.

scenes.label: Most would die
scenes.say: Wait, low-salt water? Aren't sharks supposed to die in fresh water? Most do. And that's where number three gets really weird.

scenes.label: Up the river
scenes.say: Number three. Sharks thousands of kilometers up a river, far from any ocean.

scenes.label: 1937, Illinois
scenes.say: In 1937, a fisherman near Alton, Illinois, pulled up his net. Inside was a shark. A bull shark, about five feet long and 84 pounds.

scenes.label: 1995, St. Louis
scenes.say: Illinois! That's the middle of America. And in 1995, another one was pulled out of a power plant canal just outside St. Louis.

scenes.label: 4,200 km upstream
scenes.say: Now the Amazon. Bull sharks have been recorded up to 4,200 kilometers upstream, in the foothills of the Andes in Peru.

scenes.label: Think about that
scenes.say: That's farther than New York to Los Angeles in a straight line. And they did it in a river.

scenes.label: Lake Nicaragua
scenes.say: But the best example is Lake Nicaragua. A big freshwater lake in Central America, with sharks in it.

scenes.label: Trapped forever?
scenes.say: For years, people thought those sharks were trapped in the lake forever. In 1961, they were finally identified as bull sharks.

scenes.label: Not trapped
scenes.say: But about ten years later, scientists proved they weren't trapped at all. Here's how.

scenes.label: 2,200 sharks tagged
scenes.say: In 1968 and 1969, scientists tagged more than 2,200 sharks. And the tags showed them swimming up a 190 kilometer river from the sea.

scenes.label: 10% came back
scenes.say: About ten percent of those tags came back from sharks caught again. That's how they could track the trip.

scenes.label: 7 to 11 days
scenes.say: That river has rapids. And some sharks made the whole trip in as little as seven to eleven days.

scenes.label: The secret
scenes.say: So how does a sea animal survive fresh water, when it would kill most sharks? Here's the secret. It's basically about peeing.

scenes.label: 20x the pee
scenes.say: Fresh water keeps flooding into a shark's body. So lake bull sharks make very watery urine, more than twenty times faster than sea sharks.

scenes.label: Less salty blood
scenes.say: They also run their blood less salty, with about twenty percent less sodium and chloride. It's like turning down a dial.

scenes.label: Half the urea
scenes.say: And they keep less than half the urea that sea sharks carry. That's a chemical most sharks use to hold on to water.

scenes.label: Costly trick
scenes.say: But it costs a lot of energy. That's why their babies are born where rivers meet the sea, not deep in the lake.

scenes.label: Mystery solved
scenes.say: And that explains the golf course. Bull sharks are the rare shark that can do this.

scenes.label: Out of water
scenes.say: Okay, number two. Now we leave the water completely. Well, almost.

scenes.label: About 3 feet
scenes.say: This is the epaulette shark. About three feet long, spotted, living on reefs around New Guinea and northern Australia.

scenes.label: Low tide
scenes.say: When the tide goes out, its shallow reef turns into little pools. Some dry up. Some lose their oxygen.

scenes.label: It walks
scenes.say: So what does it do? It walks. It uses its fins like legs and crawls across the reef to the next pool.

scenes.label: Like a lizard
scenes.say: Picture it. A shark, out in the air, wiggling over wet coral like a lizard. Sounds fake, right? It isn't.

scenes.label: Up to 2 hours
scenes.say: And it can survive with almost no oxygen for up to about two hours. Most sharks would be in deep trouble.

scenes.label: Baby walkers
scenes.say: Scientists from Florida Atlantic University and James Cook University in Australia have studied exactly how it walks.

scenes.label: What's weirder?
scenes.say: So that's a shark on land. Now, what could possibly be weirder than that? Let's find out.

scenes.label: Inside a volcano
scenes.say: Number one. The strangest of all. Sharks living inside an active volcano.

scenes.label: About 60 ft down
scenes.say: This is Kavachi, an underwater volcano near the Solomon Islands, in the Pacific. Its top sits only about sixty feet below the surface.

scenes.label: Very active
scenes.say: And it is very active. Eruptions there are common, with boiling lava under the sea.

scenes.label: Nothing alive?
scenes.say: So you'd think nothing could live there. That's what the scientists thought too.

scenes.label: 2015 cameras
scenes.say: In 2015, a team led by Brennan Phillips dropped cameras into the crater between eruptions. And what showed up on that footage was shocking.

scenes.label: Hammerheads!
scenes.say: Instead, they found hammerhead sharks. Scalloped hammerheads, just swimming around inside.

scenes.label: The Sharkcano
scenes.say: And silky sharks too. Plus rays. Living in what people now call the Sharkcano.

scenes.label: Acid and heat
scenes.say: Here's how harsh it is. The water is so acidic, divers got mild skin burns. It was too hot for them to get close.

scenes.label: Orange water
scenes.say: Bubbles of carbon dioxide and methane rise from the floor. The water even turns orange from iron and sulfur.

scenes.label: Nobody knows
scenes.say: So why would sharks stay there? Nobody really knows. One idea is that sharks can sense changes in the Earth's magnetic field. Maybe that helps them stay safe.

scenes.label: Blast zone
scenes.say: And the explosions don't seem to drive them off. They gather right inside the crater between eruptions.

scenes.label: Tougher than us?
scenes.say: So, a canal, a golf course, a river, dry land, and a volcano. Sharks really are tougher and weirder than most of us ever think.

scenes.label: Your turn
scenes.say: Now tell me in the comments. Which one would scare you most? And where do you think Bukangi is swimming today?

short.title: A Shark Lived in a City Canal for a Month. Why?
short.header: The shark stuck in Busan's canal
short.description: A 3-meter dusky shark nicknamed Bukangi lived in a Busan city canal for over a month and drew 1.6 million visitors, until floating nets guided her to sea on October 21. Sources: AP, AFP.

scenes.say: Why did a three-meter shark live in a city canal for a month?
In mid-September, people in Busan, South Korea, spotted a big gray fin in a man-made canal.
It was a female dusky shark. Fans named her Bukangi, and more than 1.6 million visitors came to see her.
But she wasn't seen eating. The water was getting colder. She really had to go.
Water jets failed. She swam right over the nets. Then on October 21, floating nets slowly guided her out to sea.
Experts say warming seas push warm-water sharks north. So this might happen again.
And if it does, you'll know the answer to one question. Why did a three-meter shark live in a city canal for a month?
